ML-systems design: the building blocks on real libraries

Each service in the reference design, built from what vLLM, PyTorch Distributed, Ray and containers on Kubernetes or Slurm provide today: what to call, what to configure, and where the library stops and your code starts.

Plain wordsName the part, then say what it does here

Interviewers do not reward a list of product names. “We use Ray” is not an answer; “one Ray driver owns every engine, so it can pause them all before a weight update” is. Each section below gives you that second sentence for one part of the machine.

For leadersWhere the libraries stop

vLLM generates and can be paused and updated in place; it does not tag tokens with weight versions or decide staleness. FSDP2 shards the trainer and DCP checkpoints it asynchronously; it does not know about rollouts. Ray starts and calls processes; the buffer, the staleness policy and the failure policy are your code. Sandboxes and weight sync are where most of the engineering, and most of the interview depth, sits.

§05

The rollout service on vLLM

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

How do you build the rollout fleet from vLLM, and which of its APIs does RL depend on?

Run vLLM engines as replicas (tensor parallel inside a node for dense models, data and expert parallel across 16–64 GPUs for MoE), either in-process as AsyncLLM inside Ray actors or as vllm serve behind a request router that keeps each session on one replica (sticky routing). Drive them token-in, token-out and ask for log-probs, sampling masks and routed experts. Update them with a weight-transfer engine and pause_generation(mode="keep"); colocate them with sleep mode. Twelve RL needs map onto twelve vLLM features.

Inside the engine, in one minute

vLLM is an open-source inference engine: it loads a model onto one or more GPUs and generates tokens for hundreds of requests at once. Interviewers often ask what it does inside, not only how to call it. Five facts carry the answer:

  • Three kinds of processes. An API server turns HTTP text into token IDs and streams results back; an engine core runs the scheduler and the KV-cache manager in a loop; one GPU worker per GPU holds its slice of the weights and runs the model. Keeping them apart stops Python text handling from stalling the GPUs.
  • A token budget per engine step. An engine step is one forward pass over the current batch, every few tens of milliseconds. The scheduler hands out up to 8K–16K tokens per step: one to every request that is decoding, the rest to chunks of new prompts (chunked prefill), running requests first. 78 decoding sequences take 78 tokens of an 8K budget; the rest goes to prompts. Requests join and leave the batch at every step, which is called continuous batching.
  • A paged KV cache. The memory left after the weights becomes a pool of 16-token blocks. Each request's block table lists its blocks, which can sit anywhere, so a request that stops at 2K tokens never reserved room for 64K. When no block is free, the newest running request is preempted: its blocks are freed and it is recomputed later.
  • Prefix caching by hash. Each full block gets an ID: a hash of its 16 token IDs and the previous block's ID, because a block's keys and values depend on every earlier token. A task's G samples share the prompt's blocks, and an agent's next turn prefills only its new tokens, if it reaches the same replica.
  • CUDA graphs. The hundreds of kernel launches in one engine step are recorded once and replayed in one call. The recording holds fixed memory addresses, so new weights are copied into the existing tensors, never swapped in as new ones.

Two ways to embed vLLM

In-process engines

AsyncLLM inside a Ray actor · e.g. NeMo-RL, verl

  • The engine's front end, AsyncLLM, lives inside a Ray actor, a long-lived process the driver can call (§7). There is no HTTP hop: the orchestrator awaits engine.generate() directly.
  • Weight sync and pause are method calls on the actor's handle, the driver's reference to it.
  • Ties orchestrator and engines to Python and Ray, and engine scaling to your actor code.

Servers behind a router

vllm serve + vllm-router · e.g. prime-rl, agent harnesses

  • Each replica is a vllm serve HTTP server: any harness that speaks HTTP can drive it, and replicas scale independently.
  • The router hashes each session ID to a replica (consistent hashing, so losing one replica moves only its own sessions), and every turn returns to the replica that holds its cache: sticky routing, or session affinity.
  • Each call pays a little for HTTP, and pause and sync must be sent to every server.

The RL API surface

RL needsvLLM featureHow you ask for it
Exact tokens, no re-tokenizingToken IDs in and outgenerate({"prompt_token_ids": ids}, …); HTTP /inference/v1/generate (with --enable-scale-out), or return_token_ids on the OpenAI endpoints
Behaviour log-probs μSampled-token log-probsSamplingParams(logprobs=0) returns the sampled token's own log-prob and no alternatives; logprobs_mode="processed_logprobs" reports it under the truncated distribution that was actually sampled
Top-k/top-p consistencySampling maskThe engine flag return_sampling_mask=True (--return-sampling-mask) returns, per token, the IDs that survived truncation, so the trainer normalizes over the same set. It needs processed_logprobs and Model Runner V2 (vLLM's newer GPU worker, the default on main for supported configurations), and every request must set temperature > 0 and top_k > 0: a pure top-p request is rejected
MoE consistencyRouted expertsenable_return_routed_experts=True; each output carries routed_experts of shape [tokens, layers, top-k] for routing replay
G samples per taskParallel samplingSamplingParams(n=8) shares one prefill across the group
Cheap later turnsAutomatic prefix cachingOn by default; keep each session on one replica
Updates mid-flightPause and resumeawait engine.pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=False), then resume_generation(); HTTP POST /pause?mode=keep&clear_cache=false, POST /resume. The default, clear_cache=True, drops the cache and re-prefills every running request
New weightsWeight-transfer enginesWeightTransferConfig(backend="nccl"), or "ipc", "nccl_m2n", "sharded_rdt", "sparse_nccl", "modelexpress"; the trainer drives them (§9)
Version tagsWeight versionsfinish_weight_update(weight_version=…) or POST /update_weight_version sets the engine's current version, and GET /weight_info reads it. Outputs don't carry it, so the orchestrator tags token spans
Sharing GPUs with the trainerSleep modeenable_sleep_mode=True; sleep(level=1) offloads weights and drops the KV cache, level=2 drops both; wake_up(tags=["weights"]), then ["kv_cache"]
Determinism and checksBatch invariance, weight checkerVLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 (NVIDIA compute capability 8.0 and up: A100 and newer); POST /weight_checker hashes every shard
Anything elseCollective RPCcollective_rpc("method", args=…) runs a method on every worker

These are the names on vLLM's main branch in October 2026; the weight-transfer API was rebuilt during 2026, so check the version you are given. The HTTP control endpoints need VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1 and must never face users. On main, clear_cache is already marked deprecated, in the HTTP pause route (whose docstring says keep mode ignores it) and in the EngineClient interface, while the engine still honours it, so pass it explicitly and check what your version does. SGLang offers the same shapes (update_weights_from_distributed, release_memory_occupation, pause_generation).

Sketch · one agent trajectory, token-in and token-out

from vllm import AsyncEngineArgs, SamplingParams
from vllm.config import WeightTransferConfig
from vllm.v1.engine.async_llm import AsyncLLM

engine = AsyncLLM.from_engine_args(AsyncEngineArgs(
  model="ckpt/policy-70b", tensor_parallel_size=4,
  quantization="fp8", kv_cache_dtype="fp8",
  logprobs_mode="processed_logprobs",
  weight_transfer_config=WeightTransferConfig(backend="nccl"),
))

async def rollout(task, sandbox, tok, version):
  ids = tok.apply_chat_template(task.messages, add_generation_prompt=True)
  traj = Trajectory(task_id=task.id, prompt_ids=list(ids))
  for turn in range(task.max_turns):
    params = SamplingParams(temperature=1.0, max_tokens=4096, logprobs=0,
                            stop_token_ids=[TOOL_END, tok.eos_token_id])
    async for out in engine.generate({"prompt_token_ids": ids}, params,
                                     request_id=f"{traj.id}:{turn}"):
      pass                                  # streamed; the last item has everything
    gen = out.outputs[0]
    traj.add_model(gen.token_ids, gen.logprobs, version=version())  # loss mask 1
    ids = ids + list(gen.token_ids)
    if gen.token_ids[-1] == tok.eos_token_id:
      break
    result = await sandbox.run(parse_tool_call(tok.decode(gen.token_ids)))
    obs = tok.encode(render_tool_result(result), add_special_tokens=False)
    traj.add_env(obs)                      # loss mask 0: no loss on tool output
    ids = ids + obs
  return traj

One subtlety: with mode="keep", a single generate call can straddle a weight update. The orchestrator knows when it paused, so record the token count at each pause and tag the two spans with their versions. The clear_cache flag decides what the pause costs. Its default, True, drops the prefix cache and preempts every running request, so on resume every live context is prefilled again under the new weights: for the coding run in §11 that is about 120M tokens, some 7 GPU-hours a step, a tenth of all rollout work. With False, the earlier tokens' cache entries still come from the old weights, which Magistral found acceptable. This guide assumes False.

Sizing a replica

  1. Smallest tensor-parallel size that leaves room for cache. Keep weights to a quarter or half of the replica's memory. A 70B in FP8 on H100s: TP=4 leaves about 217 GB for cache (90% of 4 × 80 GB, a little under vLLM's 92% default to leave room for activations, minus 70.6 GB of weights), 78 sequences at 17K tokens of context; TP=2 leaves 73 GB, 26 sequences.
  2. For MoE, go wide. Each engine step reads every expert's weights once, however few tokens reach it, so an expert needs many tokens per step to be worth reading. Data-parallel attention (every GPU holds the attention weights and its own requests) plus expert parallelism (each GPU holds a few experts) over 16–64 GPUs pools all those GPUs' requests into one large batch per step, and MLA keeps the cache small.
  3. Keep waiting trajectories cached. Between turns a trajectory has no running request, so its blocks sit in the free pool, kept until another request needs the room, oldest first. Watch the prefix-cache hit rate. If it falls, add a CPU KV-offload tier, which keeps a copy of each block in host memory and copies evicted ones back instead of re-prefilling (prime-rl's GLM-5 SWE recipe offloads to a distributed CPU pool of 1 TB per node).
Say it

“Rollouts are vLLM replicas at TP=4 behind a request router with sticky sessions, driven token-in and token-out so the trainer sees exactly the sampled tokens with their log-probs. New weights arrive through vLLM's NCCL weight-transfer engine while requests are frozen with pause in keep mode, and every token span is tagged with its weight version.”

§06

The trainer on PyTorch Distributed

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

How do you build the RL trainer from PyTorch's native pieces, and what does it do that an SFT trainer doesn't?

A DeviceMesh, PyTorch's named grid of GPUs (replicate × shard, optionally × tp); FSDP2, the current version of FSDP, whose fully_shard splits every parameter of each block across the shard dimension instead of flattening the block into one buffer, with BF16 compute and FP32 gradient reduction; activation checkpointing; micro-batches packed to a token budget; a loss that consumes behaviour log-probs, versions and masks; DCP's (Distributed Checkpoint's) async_save for checkpoints; and a weight source for sync. It differs from SFT in five ways: data from a queue, wildly variable lengths, an extra forward pass for πold, an importance-weighted loss, and weights that leave every step. Move to Megatron or TorchTitan when you need pipeline and expert parallelism.

What changes from SFT

ConcernSFTRL
DataA file read in a fixed orderA queue of scored groups with versions; log which trajectories made each step
LengthsPacked to a fixed length1K to 64K tokens; pack to a token budget, balance tokens across ranks, and past about 32K use context parallelism, which splits one sequence across GPUs
PassesForward and backwardPlus a forward to recompute πold, and a reference-model forward if the loss has a KL term
LossCross-entropyClipped, importance-weighted policy gradient over model tokens only, averaged per token
WeightsSaved at the endExported to the rollout fleet every step (§9)

Sketch · FSDP2 trainer step and asynchronous checkpoint

import torch, torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import init_device_mesh
from torch.distributed.fsdp import FSDPModule, fully_shard, MixedPrecisionPolicy
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import get_state_dict

dist.init_process_group("cpu:gloo,cuda:nccl")  # async_save needs a CPU backend
mesh = init_device_mesh("cuda", (9, 80), mesh_dim_names=("replicate", "shard"))
mp = MixedPrecisionPolicy(param_dtype=torch.bfloat16, reduce_dtype=torch.float32)
for block in model.layers:                  # bottom-up: one all-gather group per block
  fully_shard(block, mesh=mesh, mp_policy=mp)
fully_shard(model, mesh=mesh, mp_policy=mp)
for m in model.modules():                   # the loss already divides by the step's token
  if isinstance(m, FSDPModule):             # count, so sum gradients across ranks
    m.set_gradient_divide_factor(1.0)       # instead of averaging them
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-6)

def micro_step(mb, step_tokens):            # mb: packed trajectories, one token budget
  logp = token_logprobs(model, mb)          # [tokens], varlen attention, FP32 log-softmax
  ratio = torch.exp(logp - mb.logp_old)     # π_θ / π_old (recomputed)
  tis = torch.exp(mb.logp_old - mb.logp_mu).clamp(max=2.0)  # π_old / μ, truncated
  pg = torch.minimum(ratio * mb.adv, ratio.clamp(0.8, 1.28) * mb.adv)
  loss = -(tis * pg * mb.mask).sum() / step_tokens  # model tokens in the step, all ranks
  loss.backward()

def optim_step():
  torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
  opt.step()
  opt.zero_grad()

def save(step):                             # blocks only for the copy to host memory
  msd, osd = get_state_dict(model, opt)
  return dcp.async_save({"model": msd, "optim": osd, "step": step},
                        checkpoint_id=f"/ckpt/{RUN}/step-{step:06d}")

DCP writes each rank's shards in parallel and can reload them onto a different number of GPUs, which is what lets you restart a failed job on a smaller or larger trainer. For sync, vLLM's ModuleSource(model) walks an FSDP2 model and all-gathers one parameter at a time with full_tensor(); every rank must take part because the gather is collective, and only rank 0 puts bytes on the wire (§9).

Knobs that matter

KnobWhat it tradesSetting for the coding run
reshard_after_forwardMemory against a second all-gather in backwardTrue for blocks, False for the root
Activation checkpointingAbout 30% more compute against activation memoryOn for every block at 32K tokens
Token budget per micro-batchMemory against kernel efficiency16K–32K tokens per GPU, packed with varlen attention. With every block checkpointed a 70B still keeps about 1.3 MB per token (40 GiB at 32K), so the longest trajectories need context parallelism
Shard-group sizeCollective locality against memory per GPUShard inside a node or rack, replicate across
Log-prob precisionMismatch against memoryFP32 LM head and log-softmax for policy log-probs
reduce_dtypeStability against bandwidthFP32 gradient reduction

When to leave FSDP2

FSDP2 alone is simple and fast for dense models up to roughly 100B. Beyond that, and for MoE, you need expert parallelism and usually pipeline parallelism: Megatron-Core (the backend in NeMo-RL, slime and verl's Megatron path) or TorchTitan, which composes FSDP2 with tensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism natively and checkpoints asynchronously. Cohere's FAX expresses the same mesh ideas in JAX, where the GSPMD compiler partitions each operation.

Say it

“The trainer is FSDP2 on a (9, 80) mesh: each group of 80 GPUs holds one sharded copy of the model, and the nine copies combine their gradients with an all-reduce. It differs from SFT in five ways: a queue instead of a file, sequences of 1K to 64K tokens packed to a token budget, an extra forward pass for πold, an importance-weighted token-mean loss, and weights exported every step. Checkpoints are DCP asynchronous saves that block training for about a second.”

§07

The orchestrator and data flow on Ray

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

Who starts and connects all these processes, and how does data move between them without anyone blocking?

One controller program, a Ray driver, owns the loop. Ray actors wrap engines, trainer ranks and environment clients, and placement groups reserve GPUs: shared bundles when colocated, separate groups for split pools. A bounded, versioned buffer decouples rollouts from training and applies backpressure; the trajectory record is the contract between them. Control messages travel as Ray calls; large tensors travel over NCCL, NIXL or storage, never through the CPU object store. A dense trajectory is about 290 KB; a 235B MoE's routed experts add 24 MB more.

Ray in five points

Ray is a Python library that turns one script, the driver, into the controller of a cluster: it starts processes on other machines and calls their methods as if they were local objects. torchrun works the other way round: every GPU runs its own copy of the same script.

  • Actors and tasks. @ray.remote on a class makes an actor, a long-lived process that keeps its state (a vLLM engine with its weights and cache, or one trainer rank); on a function it makes a task, a stateless call that runs wherever resources are free.
  • Futures. Every .remote() call returns at once with an ObjectRef, a future; ray.get waits for one result and ray.wait for the first of many, which is how one driver keeps thousands of trajectories in flight.
  • Placement. num_gpus=1 asks for a GPU. A placement group reserves several bundles at once, all or nothing. A bundle is a set of resources that must fit on one node, such as {"GPU": 8, "CPU": 64}, and the group is packed onto few nodes (PACK) or spread (SPREAD), so a gang of actors lands where you planned or not at all.
  • Data. Results land in an object store in CPU shared memory: fine for a 290 KB trajectory, slow for gigabytes of GPU tensors. Those go GPU to GPU over NCCL or NIXL; Ray Direct Transport (RDT) does this for calls between actors (@ray.method(tensor_transport="nixl")), with Gloo for CPU tensors.
  • Failures. If an actor's process dies, the driver's next call to it raises an error. Ray restarts it only if it was created with max_restarts above 0, and even then its weights and cache are gone, so the driver decides what happens to its work. This single-controller style, one driver that sees the whole loop, is what verl's HybridFlow design is built on.

Three layers, and who uses Ray

Ray is often confused with Kubernetes and with torch.distributed. They stack, and one sentence covers it: Kubernetes runs the cluster, Ray coordinates the job, NCCL moves the tensors.

Kubernetes or SlurmRaytorch.distributed
Managesmachines, and the containers or jobs on themthe processes and calls inside one jobtensor traffic between GPUs
Unita pod or job, seconds to minutes to starta task or actor, milliseconds to schedule a taska collective, such as an all-reduce
Doesn'tknow what your programs do, or move their datamove GPU tensors quicklystart processes or run different programs

What Ray buys you here: one Python program starts 76 engine replicas and 720 trainer ranks with the GPUs each needs, places each pool as a gang, calls any of them and waits on thousands of replies at once, and finds out when one dies. It is the most common controller, not the only one. In their current source, about half of the open RL libraries are built on it: verl, NeMo-RL, OpenRLHF, open-instruct, SkyRL, ROLL, slime and Miles. prime-rl, PipelineRL and TRL run plain processes: torchrun or accelerate for the trainer, and vLLM as a separate server or, in TRL's colocate mode for vLLM, inside the trainer's own processes. TorchForge uses PyTorch's own actor framework, Monarch, and Meta's LlamaRL is a single controller in plain PyTorch. So name the pattern first, one controller with a handle on every worker, then Ray as one way to get it.

Sketch · a trainer gang and the asynchronous loop

import asyncio, ray
from ray.util.placement_group import placement_group
from ray.util.scheduling_strategies import PlacementGroupSchedulingStrategy

ray.init(address="auto")
train_pg = placement_group([{"GPU": 8, "CPU": 64}] * 90, strategy="PACK")
ray.get(train_pg.ready())                   # all 90 nodes or none: a gang
ranks = [TrainerRank.options(num_gpus=1, scheduling_strategy=PlacementGroupSchedulingStrategy(
           placement_group=train_pg, placement_group_bundle_index=r // 8)).remote(rank=r)
         for r in range(720)]

async def produce(tasks, engines, buffer, slots):
  async def one(task):
    try:
      group = await asyncio.gather(*(run_trajectory(task, engines.pick(task)) for _ in range(8)))
      await buffer.put(Group(task, group))  # waits while the buffer is full
    finally:
      slots.release()
  running = set()                           # hold references, or tasks can be collected
  for task in tasks:
    await slots.acquire()                   # caps groups in flight
    t = asyncio.create_task(one(task))
    running.add(t)
    t.add_done_callback(running.discard)

async def consume(trainer, buffer, sync, max_lag=4):
  while True:
    batch = await buffer.take(groups=1024, min_version=sync.version - max_lag)
    await trainer.step(batch)               # one call fans out to all 720 ranks
    await sync.publish()                    # pause(keep), send_weights, bump version, resume

The trajectory record

FieldExampleWhy it exists
Trajectory and group IDst-81f3 · task-2291Join the G samples of a task; make retries idempotent
Task and image versionsswe-tasks@2026-09 · sha256:9c1…Rebuild the exact environment later
Token IDsint32 [32K]Train on exactly what was sampled
Loss maskuint8 [32K]Model tokens 1, prompt and tool tokens 0
Behaviour log-probs μfloat32 [32K]Importance weights
Version spans(0, 9.4K, v41) · (9.4K, 12.5K, v42)Staleness filter and per-token correction
Routed experts (MoE)uint8 [32K, 94, 8] ≈ 24 MBRouting replay in the trainer
Reward, parts, status1.0 · {tests: 1, format: 0} · okVoid, not zero, on infrastructure failure; debugging
Reward function versionhidden_tests@v3Compare runs; roll back bad reward changes
Timingsqueue · generate · tool · scoreFind the slow stage

A dense 32K-token trajectory is about 290 KB. A 235B MoE's routed experts add about 24 MB per trajectory, 200 GB per step of 8,192, so they travel on a side channel straight to the trainer instead of through the driver.

Buffer rules

  • Bounded. When it is full, producers wait. Backpressure keeps stale data from piling up.
  • Group-complete. Group-relative advantages need all G samples, so a group is released only when every sample is scored or void; if too many are void, the group is dropped.
  • Staleness filter. Drop or down-weight groups more than K versions old.
  • Windowed FIFO. Look only at a small window at the head of the queue, in submission order, and take whichever groups in it have finished; later groups wait their turn, so batches don't skew toward the short trajectories that finish first.
  • Dynamic sampling. Drop groups whose rewards are all equal, since they carry no gradient, and count them as waste.
Say it

“One Ray driver owns the loop. Every engine replica and trainer rank is an actor, a long-lived process I hold a handle to, and placement groups reserve each pool's GPUs all at once. Control calls go through Ray; weights go GPU to GPU over NCCL, never through Ray's CPU object store. Kubernetes gives the job its machines, Ray coordinates it, and NCCL moves the tensors.”

§08

Sandboxes and rewards as services

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

How do you run thousands of sandboxes executing untrusted, model-written code, plus the reward checks, as services, and what are their APIs?

An environment API (reset, step, close) in front of a sandbox pool on its own CPU cluster: one Docker container per live trajectory, started from per-task images of 1–2.5 GB, with warm pools, image caches, prepare-once-and-fork for the G samples of a task, hard resource limits and no network egress. The isolation choice is the container runtime: plain runc, which most open stacks run and which is defensible on dedicated, egress-blocked nodes, or gVisor or a microVM when sandboxes share nodes with other teams' work, need network access or root, or face a policy strong enough that an escape is a plausible reward hack. Rewards run as a separate service (unit-test verifiers, LLM judges) that returns a score with a status, so an infrastructure failure voids a sample instead of scoring it zero. Little's law sizes the pool: about 7,100 sandboxes and 14,000 vCPUs for the 1,024-GPU coding run.

Docker in one paragraph

A container is not a virtual machine. It is an ordinary Linux process that the operating system's kernel (the Linux kernel, not a GPU kernel) fences off: namespaces give it its own view of the filesystem, the process list and the network, and cgroups cap its CPU and memory, so it starts in about a second. Every container on a node shares that one kernel and asks it for everything through system calls: open a file, start a process, open a socket. Its files come from an image, a stack of read-only layers built from a Dockerfile and pulled from a registry; a SWE task is one image per repository snapshot with its dependencies installed. Docker builds and runs images through a background service on each node, the Docker daemon; underneath, a small program called the runtime starts the process, runc by default. The same image runs under Kubernetes, and under a stronger runtime when you need one, so “Docker or gVisor” is a false choice: it is Docker images either way, and the runtime is the decision.

Interfaces · environment, sandbox pool, reward

class Env(Protocol):
  async def reset(self, task: TaskSpec, seed: int) -> Observation: ...
  async def step(self, call: ToolCall) -> StepResult: ...       # observation, done, info
  async def close(self) -> None: ...

class SandboxPool(Protocol):
  async def acquire(self, image: str, cpu: float, mem_gb: int, ttl_s: int) -> Sandbox: ...
  async def fork(self, sb: Sandbox, n: int) -> list[Sandbox]: ... # prepare once, copy G times
  async def release(self, sb: Sandbox) -> None: ...

class Sandbox(Protocol):
  async def run(self, cmd: list[str], timeout_s: int) -> ExecResult: ...  # stdout, stderr, exit
  async def write(self, path: str, data: bytes) -> None: ...

class Reward(Protocol):
  async def score(self, traj: Trajectory) -> RewardResult: ...  # value, parts, status, version

Pick the runtime from the threat model

RuntimeMechanismCostUse when
runc, Docker's defaultNamespaces and cgroups on the shared host kernelStarts in about a second from a cached image; near-zero overheadDedicated sandbox nodes with egress blocked and nothing worth stealing. Most open RL-for-code stacks run runc (SWE-bench's harness, R2E-Gym, DeepSWE). The risk is a kernel or runtime bug
gVisor (runsc)A second kernel, written as an ordinary program, intercepts the sandbox's system calls and serves them itself, so the code never talks to the host kernel directly; gVisor itself makes only a small, filtered set of host callsSimilar start time; slower on system-call-heavy work such as buildsSandboxes that share nodes with other teams' work or tenants; what Modal runs. Same images: docker run --runtime=runsc
MicroVMs (Firecracker, Kata)Each sandbox runs its own kernel inside a small virtual machine, walled off by the CPU's virtualization hardwareFirecracker boots in about 125 ms; a little memory per VMThe strongest boundary, for sandboxes that need network access or root, or that run external customers' code; E2B's sandboxes are Firecracker VMs

Whatever the runtime: deny network egress except to internal package mirrors (which also stops a few thousand sandboxes from hammering public registries), cap CPU, memory, processes, disk and wall-clock time, mount the base image read-only, and never put credentials inside.

Startup is the hidden cost

Preparing a SWE environment took about 90 s per instance with Docker in the SWE-MiniSandbox measurements, and per-task images are large: SWE-bench Verified needs 605 GB for 500 tasks, SWE-Gym about 6 TB for 2,400, while SWE-smith shares images and fits 50,000 tasks in 295 GB. Four fixes, cheapest first: prefetch images for the next steps' tasks (the task schedule is known in advance), keep warm pools per image, prepare each task once and start its G copies from the prepared state, and build task images as thin layers on shared bases.

Rewards as a service

  • Hidden tests. Copy the tests into the sandbox only at grading time, so the policy can neither read nor edit them, and parse the results into pass/fail and partial credit.
  • Status with every score. Each result is {value, parts, status, version}, and the status says whose fault a bad outcome was: ok (including a policy that ran out of turns or time, which scores zero), infra_error (a lost node, a failed image pull, a judge timeout) or invalid (a broken task). Only ok enters the loss; the others are void.
  • Idempotent. Key every request by trajectory ID so a retry never double-counts.
  • Versioned and tested. Version every reward function and keep a golden set of trajectories with known rewards; run it on every change.

Sizing

Apply Little's law per stage. Sandboxes = λ × trajectory lifetime; tool calls per second = trajectories in flight × turns ÷ lifetime; verifier CPU = λ × test time. For the coding run, λ = 10.6 per second and each trajectory lives 674 s, so about 7,100 sandboxes are alive and they make 264 tool calls per second. At 2 vCPUs and 4 GB each that is 14,000 vCPUs and 28 TB of memory, about 75 CPU nodes: cheap next to 1,024 GPUs, but a cluster with its own on-call. DeepSWE is a useful smaller anchor: 64 GPUs drove 512 concurrent containers, on nodes with 200 CPUs and 6 TB of disk, once one node's Docker daemon proved too small and Kubernetes spread the containers across a pool.

Say it

“Each trajectory gets a Docker container from its task's image, on a separate CPU cluster: about 7,100 at once, by Little's law. Docker is the packaging and the runtime is the isolation: runc on these dedicated, egress-blocked nodes, gVisor if the pool is shared with other teams. Startup is the real cost, so I prefetch images, keep warm pools and start the 8 samples of a task from one prepared copy. Every reward carries a status, and infrastructure failures are void, not zero.”

§09

The weight-sync service

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

How do new weights get from the trainer to the fleet quickly and safely, and what does a versioned protocol look like?

Three phases. Stage: pause the engines with requests frozen (or keep generating if a second copy of the weights fits), move the bytes, and convert them to the engine's layout, joining the trainer's separate q, k and v matrices (and gate and up) into the engine's fused ones and quantizing to FP8. Commit: wait until every GPU of every replica acknowledges. Flip: bump the version and resume. vLLM's weight-transfer engine runs this as one init call at start-up, then start, update and finish at every sync, over six transports (the table below). The three to know are CUDA IPC when colocated, an NCCL broadcast for split pools (70B in BF16 in about 3.5 s) and sharded RDMA pulls for large MoE, where each GPU fetches only its slice. Check every sync with checksums and canary log-probs (the Field Guide's parity probe).

Six transports

BackendHow the bytes moveUse whenTime
ipcCUDA IPC handles: the engine reads the trainer's GPU memory directlyColocated on the same GPUsNo copy over a network; chunks bound the memory
ncclTrainer rank 0 packs parameters into 1 GiB buckets and broadcasts them to every engine worker, filling the next bucket while one is on the wireSplit pools, dense models up to about 100BAbout S ÷ b: 70B in BF16, 3.5 s
nccl_m2nOne reshard collective per parameter between the trainer's mesh and the engine'sDifferent layouts (FSDP to TP) without gathering full tensors. Fused and quantized parameters fall back to full tensors, which caps a sharded trainer at 16 ranksAbout each GPU's shard ÷ b for parameters that map directly
sharded_rdtEngines pull only their slices over NIXL (RDMA), one layer group at a time, from a producer actor beside each trainer rankLarge MoE served with expert parallelism; pipeline-parallel trainers. Needs engine workers that are Ray actors, and NIXLAbout each engine GPU's slice ÷ b: 28 GB ÷ 40 GB/s ≈ 0.7 s for the 1T MoE of §13
sparse_ncclBroadcast only the values that changed, as (position, value) pairs in the checkpoint's own tensor names and shapes, before any fusingFew values change; per-expert updatesProportional to changed values
modelexpressInstall immutable published versions, pulled GPU to GPU over NIXL from trainer ranks or peers that hold them, or from storage when no peer doesElastic fleets, recovery, a trainer decoupled from the fleetSeconds from GPU peers, minutes from storage

Sketch · trainer side, every rank

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer import (
  HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient, ModuleSource, WeightTransferTrainerFactory)
from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer.nccl_engine import NCCLTrainerInitInfo

class Fleet:                                          # vLLM's client protocol: these four methods
  def __init__(self, urls, tp):
    self.servers = [HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient(u) for u in urls]
    self.tp, self.pool = tp, ThreadPoolExecutor(len(urls))
  def _all(self, call):                               # every server at once: NCCL waits for all
    list(self.pool.map(call, range(len(self.servers)), self.servers))
  def init_weight_transfer_engine(self, info):        # each server numbers its workers from 1,
    self._all(lambda i, s: s.init_weight_transfer_engine(
      {**info, "rank_offset": 1 + i * self.tp}))      # so give each its own block of ranks
  def start_weight_update(self):
    self._all(lambda i, s: s.start_weight_update())
  def update_weights(self, info):
    self._all(lambda i, s: s.update_weights(info))
  def finish_weight_update(self, weight_version=None):
    self._all(lambda i, s: s.finish_weight_update(weight_version))

engine = WeightTransferTrainerFactory.trainer_init(   # once, before training
  init_info=NCCLTrainerInitInfo(
    master_address=ADDR, master_port=PORT,
    world_size=1 + 76 * 4,                            # rank 0 plus all 304 engine workers
    rank=dist.get_rank(), packed=True),               # rank 0 sends; others join gathers
  client=Fleet(ENGINE_URLS, tp=4),
  source=ModuleSource(model),                         # FSDP2: full_tensor() per parameter
)

def publish(version):                                 # every rank, after each optimizer step
  if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    post_all("/pause?mode=keep&clear_cache=false")    # freeze requests, keep their cache
  engine.send_weights()                               # start, update (broadcast), finish
  if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    post_all("/update_weight_version", {"new_version": str(version)})
    post_all("/resume")

Each vLLM server numbers its workers from rank 1, so independent servers can share one NCCL group only if the client gives each server its own block of ranks, which is what Fleet does (OpenRLHF uses the same offsets). Run the 76 replicas as one deployment with internal data parallelism (--data-parallel-size 76) instead, and vLLM numbers the workers itself, so one HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient and one pause reach every engine. The price is one failure domain for the whole fleet, because vLLM's fault-tolerance mode works only with an external load balancer.

Making it fast

  • FP8 on the wire halves the bytes. Either quantize on the trainer, storing one scale factor per 128 × 128 block so each block uses FP8's narrow range well, or let the engine quantize as its own loaders install each layer.
  • Pipeline by layer. Gather layer i+1 while layer i is on the wire, with a bound on how many layers are in memory.
  • Spread the senders. Every trainer rank sends its own shard instead of rank 0 sending everything.
  • Keep sync traffic off the trainer's links, with separate network cards (NICs) or a lower-priority traffic class on the same ones, so it doesn't stall FSDP's collectives.
  • Double-buffer when memory allows: stage the new weights beside the old, then copy them into place in a sub-second pause; swapping pointers instead would break the engine's captured CUDA graphs.

Reference points: Perplexity moves Kimi-K2 (1T) from 256 training GPUs to 128 inference GPUs in 1.3 s with RDMA writes; Moonshot's checkpoint-engine updates Kimi-K2 in FP8 on 256 H20s (NVIDIA's export-market Hopper GPU) in about 16 s by broadcast (its point-to-point mode, about 17 s, is for adding new instances); Magistral pushes weights over NCCL in under 5 s without discarding in-flight sequences.

Say it

“After each optimizer step the coordinator pauses every engine with its requests and cache kept. The trainer streams the weights layer by layer, each replica installs them in place and acknowledges, and only then does the version flip and generation resume: about 3.5 s for a 70B over NCCL. The orchestrator tags every token span with its version, and checksums and canary log-probs verify each sync.”

§10

The control plane

What runs around the training loop to keep a shared GPU cluster busy, healthy and debuggable?

A scheduler with all-or-nothing admission and quotas (Kubernetes with Kueue, or Slurm); preemption that checkpoints when the job receives SIGTERM, the polite stop signal that arrives a grace period (30 s by default on Kubernetes) before the kill; health checks and automatic restarts, where rollout replicas are replaceable and the trainer is not; asynchronous checkpoints at the Young–Daly interval; telemetry at three levels (system, RL dynamics, per-trajectory traces); every change released to part of the fleet first; and cost tracked as GPU-hours per useful token.

Kubernetes in one paragraph

Kubernetes runs containers on a fleet of machines, working from declarations. A node is a machine; a pod is one or more containers that run together on one node, and it is the unit Kubernetes places. You declare what should exist, say 76 rollout pods of one image with 4 GPUs each, and controllers keep reality matching it: when a node dies and its two pods vanish, two new ones start elsewhere. Operators are add-ons that teach Kubernetes new kinds of objects: KubeRay runs Ray clusters, JobSet runs a group of pods as one job, and LeaderWorkerSet runs multi-node inference replicas. A namespace is a team's folder of objects with its own permissions. What training needs and Kubernetes lacks is gangs: the default scheduler places pods one at a time, so two trainers can each get half their GPUs and wait forever. Kueue adds queues, quotas and all-or-nothing admission.

Kueue vocabulary

TermMeaningUse here
ResourceFlavorA kind of node: reserved H100, spot H100 (cheaper, but the cloud can take it back at any time), CPUSeparate GPU and sandbox capacity
ClusterQueueA pool of quota with sharing rulesOne per team or workload class
CohortClusterQueues that lend each other unused quotaTeams borrow idle GPUs
LocalQueueA team's entry point into its ClusterQueue, inside the team's namespaceWhere a team submits jobs
WorkloadPriorityClassPriority used only for queueing and preemptionProduction above exploration
All-or-nothing admissionAdmit a job only when every pod fitsTrainer gangs
Topology-aware schedulingPlace pods close together in the networkKeep a trainer inside one rack or block
PreemptionEvict lower-priority or borrowing workloads, once a ClusterQueue turns it on (the default is never)Reclaim quota quickly

How the pieces fit: the code team's ClusterQueue guarantees 1,024 reserved H100s and the math team's 512, both in one cohort. The math team submits a 720-GPU trainer while the code team uses only 300 GPUs, so Kueue admits it on borrowed quota, all 720 GPUs at once. When the code team then submits its own 720-GPU trainer, Kueue preempts the borrower, because the code team's ClusterQueue sets preemption.reclaimWithinCohort to Any (the default, Never, would leave the new trainer waiting); the borrower checkpoints on SIGTERM and requeues. Spot capacity suits rollout replicas, not trainers.

The other common choice is Slurm, the batch scheduler of most supercomputer-style GPU clusters. It has no pods: you submit a job script with sbatch asking for, say, 90 nodes of 8 GPUs, the job waits in a partition's queue (a partition is a named pool of nodes) until all 90 are free, and then srun starts your processes on every node at once, so gangs come by default. QOS levels set priorities and limits, and preemption works there too. Labs start torchrun or a Ray cluster inside a Slurm allocation, or run Ray on Kubernetes. Either way, schedule the two pools differently: trainer gangs need contiguous, high-bandwidth placement, while rollout replicas are independent, can soak up idle capacity anywhere and are the first thing to preempt.

Failure handling

FailureDetectRecoverCost
GPU or node under a rollout replicaHealth checks (DCGM, NVIDIA's GPU health tool; Xid error codes from the NVIDIA driver), request errorsRouter drops the replica; restart it elsewhere; re-queue its trajectoriesMinutes of one replica's work
Trainer rankNCCL timeout, process exitRestart the gang from the last checkpoint, or, with torchft, let one data-parallel replica drop out and rejoin without restarting the restUp to one checkpoint interval plus the restart
Hang without an errorStep-time watchdog; PyTorch's NCCL flight recorder, which logs each rank's last collectives so you can see who hungKill, exclude the node, restartThe hang, unless the watchdog is tight
Sandbox crash, or a sandbox that stops respondingEnvironment statusVoid the sample; retry the taskOne trajectory
Verifier or judge overloadTimeouts, queue depthBack off, then voidLate samples
Silent data corruption: a GPU computes wrong numbers without raising an errorLoss spikes, NaNs, cross-replica checksumsRoll back to a clean checkpointThe steps since corruption
Storage outageFailed savesKeep training, retry, alertRisk rather than time

A command the policy runs past its time limit is not an infrastructure failure: the sandbox returns a timeout observation, and a trajectory past its turn or time cap scores zero (§8). Rollout replicas are cattle and the trainer is a pet. At 4,096 GPUs you lose a rollout replica about every other day and the trainer about once a day (§12); design so the first costs nothing and the second costs one checkpoint interval. An RL checkpoint holds the sharded trainer state (DCP), the data-loader and task-sampler state, RNG seeds, the weight-version counter, curriculum and pass-rate statistics, and the resolved run config. It skips in-flight trajectories, which are cheaper to regenerate.

Telemetry at three levels

  • System

    is the machine healthy?

    GPU utilization and memory, NVLink and network counters, tokens/s per replica, KV-cache use and prefix-hit rate, queue depths, sandbox pool size and error rate, failures by type.

  • RL dynamics

    is learning healthy?

    Reward and pass rate per task family, response length, entropy, importance-weight mean, maximum and clip fraction, staleness histogram, engine-versus-trainer k3 KL, gradient norm.

  • Traces

    what happened to this sample?

    One trace per trajectory with spans for generate, tool, score and train, keyed by trajectory ID, plus a viewer that shows the tokens next to their rewards.

Alert on reward collapse, length explosion, a jump in k3 KL or clip fraction, staleness beyond its cap, and a rising sandbox error rate. Change the running system the way you would change a production service: version everything (code, images, reward functions, judge models, tokenizer and chat template), keep a small golden run whose curves must match, canary changes on part of the fleet, and keep configs reproducible. Track cost as GPU-hours per useful token: tokens that reached a gradient after void samples, all-equal groups and stale drops are removed.

Say it

“Kubernetes with Kueue runs the cluster. Each team's queue has a quota, idle quota is lent out and, with reclaim turned on, taken back by preemption, and a trainer is admitted only when all 720 of its GPUs fit. Rollout replicas are cattle: preempt them first and replace them in minutes. The trainer is a pet: at 720 GPUs it is interrupted about every three days, so I checkpoint it asynchronously every step.”
